stories.title: From the Mayflower to Texas
stories.dek: Edward Doty crossed on the Mayflower in 1620. His descendants spent two centuries in New Jersey before one of them headed west.
places: Piscataway, Middlesex County, New Jersey, USA
Scotch Plains, Union County, New Jersey, USA
Long Branch, Monmouth County, New Jersey, USA
stories.html:
Edward Doty was one of the 102 passengers on the Mayflower in 1620. He came as a servant of Stephen Hopkins and signed the Mayflower Compact. The next year he and another servant, Edward Leister, fought what is remembered as the colony's first duel. Both men were wounded, and the colony punished them for it.

Doty became a free man and a landowner in Plymouth. In 1635 he married Faith Clarke, who had come from Ipswich, Suffolk as a girl. He died in Plymouth on 23 August 1655, and Faith lived on until 1675.

Their son Samuel Doty, born in Plymouth about 1643, moved to Piscataway in East Jersey. He married there in 1678, and the family stayed in New Jersey for the next five generations, spelling the name Doty or Doughty:

  • Samuel Doty, born in Piscataway in 1679
  • Moses Doughty, born 1702, who died at Scotch Plains in 1775, on the eve of the Revolution
  • Mercy Doty, who married Reuben Compton about 1759
  • William Compton and his daughter Mary Ann Compton, who married Samuel A. Drake in 1828

Their son Joseph Cullen Drake was born at Long Branch on the Jersey Shore in 1834. He broke the pattern. He married in Illinois and died in Hamilton County, Texas, in 1904. His daughter Susie married Mark R. Winters.

What's proven: Edward Doty's Mayflower history and his son Samuel's move to Piscataway are well documented. The General Society of Mayflower Descendants publishes verified Doty lineages. In our tree, the links from Samuel down to the Comptons and Drakes don't yet cite records. Matching them against the Society's published Doty lineage is the next step.

stories.title: How Feigenwinter became Winters
stories.dek: A Swiss family from a village near Basel. Its American branch shortened the name in North Carolina.
places: Salisbury, Rowan County, North Carolina, USA
stories.html:
The Feigenwinters lived in Reinach, a village just south of Basel, for generations. The tree traces them to Heinrich Feigenwinter, born in 1636. One of the attached documents is a page from a published Feigenwinter family book.

Christoph "Stoffel" Feigenwinter was born in Reinach in 1752. He came to the North Carolina piedmont, where many Swiss and German families settled. In 1785 he married Barbara Faw, whose own family had come from the Basel area as Pfau. Christoph died at Salisbury, in Rowan County, in 1809.

Their son Henry was born in Salisbury in 1791. He served with the North Carolina militia in the War of 1812. The muster rolls and his later application spell his name "Henry Figinwinters", and one record gives it as Henry F. Winters. That is the first time the family name appears in its short form.

Henry is in Rowan County in the 1830 census. He died in Tippah County, Mississippi, in December 1845.

George Thomas Winters was born in Alabama in 1832. He was in Tippah County in 1850 and again in 1870, and by 1880 he had moved his family to Coryell County, Texas. He died at Evant, Texas, in 1908.

What's proven: Henry's War of 1812 service and George Thomas's census trail are documented. The key link, Henry as George Thomas's father, still needs a record that names them together. A probate file for Henry in Tippah County would be a good place to start. The Swiss generations come from other people's trees and need checking against the Reinach church records.

stories.title: The postmaster of Stringtown
stories.dek: The Winters family reached Indian Territory just as it became Oklahoma, and stayed in Atoka County for half a century.
places: Justice Precinct 4, Lampasas County, Texas, USA
Poteau, Le Flore County, Oklahoma, USA
stories.html:
Mark R. Winters was born in Mississippi in 1869. As a boy he moved with his family to central Texas. He was in Coryell County in 1880 and in Lampasas County in 1900 with his wife Susie and their children.

Before 1910 they moved north to Stringtown, in Atoka County, Oklahoma. Oklahoma had become a state in November 1907. On 28 November 1908, Mark was appointed postmaster of Stringtown, which the U.S. postmaster appointment records confirm. The family stayed in Stringtown through the 1940 census.

Their son Marion P. Winters was born in Texas in 1896. He registered for the World War I draft in Atoka County. The Army Transport Service passenger lists show him shipping out of New York on 20 June 1918, headed overseas with the Army. He came home and married Ina Perry, and they were back in Stringtown by 1935.

Marion and Ina's son Richard Lee Winters was born in November 1926. He grew up in Stringtown and registered for the draft there in 1946. On 7 July 1951 he married Joyce Yvonne Creamer in Durant, where she had been born. They later lived in Poteau, in Le Flore County.

What's proven: Every step here is backed by census, draft, postmaster or passenger records.

stories.title: Killed at Tippecanoe
stories.dek: John "Jack" Callahan died in the battle that set the stage for the War of 1812.
places: Battle Ground, Tippecanoe County, Indiana, USA
stories.html:
Before dawn on 7 November 1811, warriors of the confederacy led by the Shawnee brothers Tecumseh and Tenskwatawa ("the Prophet") attacked Governor William Henry Harrison's army. Harrison's men were camped near Prophetstown, on the Tippecanoe River in Indiana Territory. Harrison held the field, but dozens of his men were killed. The battle hardened the frontier against Britain, who were seen as backing the confederacy, and helped bring on the War of 1812.

According to the family tree, John "Jack" C. Callahan, born about 1765, was among the dead. His daughter Lavica Jane had married George R. Haley in Rockcastle County, Kentucky, two years earlier. The Haleys later settled in Warren County, Tennessee, and their daughter Rhoda carried the line into the Smithson and Hale families of Cannon and DeKalb counties.

What's proven: Nothing yet. No record in the tree confirms Jack Callahan's death at Tippecanoe. Harrison's army was mostly U.S. regulars and Indiana and Kentucky militia, and their casualty lists survive. Finding his name on one of them would confirm the story.

stories.title: The Chief Red Bird tradition
stories.dek: A family story connects the Brocks to a Cherokee leader. Here is what we know and what we don't.
places: Red Bird, Clay County, Kentucky, USA
stories.html:
Many family trees, ours included, say that Aaron Brock was the Cherokee leader known as Chief Red Bird, or Totsu'hwa. The Red Bird River in Clay County, Kentucky, is named for Red Bird, and the tree has Aaron dying there in 1820. His daughter Mahala "Sukey" Brock is listed as the mother of Lavica Jane Callahan.

Stories like this are common in Appalachian families, and they deserve respect as family memory. Researchers who have studied this one have not found a record showing that Aaron Brock and the Cherokee Red Bird were the same man. Accounts of Red Bird describe a Cherokee who was killed in Kentucky in the 1790s. The birthplace in the tree, "Overhills, Great Tellico, Cherokee Nation, Cumberland County, Virginia", combines places hundreds of miles apart.

The tree includes a "Native American Application" filed by a relative, Ruthie Rawlings. Applications like that (for example to the Eastern Cherokee rolls, around 1906–1909) record what families believed at the time and how the government ruled on each claim. Reading it would tell us where this tradition came from.

What's proven: This is family tradition, not documented fact. A DNA test can't confirm it either, because one ancestor from that long ago leaves too little DNA to detect.

stories.title: A captain on the Georgia frontier
stories.dek: John Stewart was killed in a raid in the first year of Wilkes County, Georgia. His son fought in the Continental Line.
places: New Bern, Craven County, North Carolina, USA
Six Mile, Pickens County, South Carolina, USA
stories.html:
Captain John Stewart was born in New Bern, North Carolina, in 1720. He moved his family to the Georgia backcountry, which became Wilkes County in 1777. Wilkes County was the edge of the colony, and the Revolution there was also a war with the Cherokee and Creek nations.

According to notes in the original tree, Capt. Stewart was killed by a raiding party on 17 December 1777. Nine years later, in 1786, his sons filed a claim against the new state government of Georgia.

His son Robert Weston Stewart, born in 1749, served as a lieutenant in the Continental Line from 1776. He lived until 1835 and died at Six Mile, in the upper country of South Carolina. Robert's granddaughter Elizabeth Fannie Stewart married into the Creamer family of Lincoln County, Georgia.

What's proven: The death and the 1786 claim come from notes copied into the tree, without a citation. Georgia's colonial and state records, and the Revolutionary War pension files, are where to confirm them. The line above Capt. Stewart goes back to "Sir John Stewart, 4th Baronet" and Lady Jane Douglas. It has impossible dates and no sources, so it is marked unproven.

stories.title: Sicily to Kansas City and Denver
stories.dek: The Palmisano family came from Termini Imerese, a fishing and market town on Sicily's north coast.
places: Kansas City, Jackson County, Missouri, USA
stories.html:
Termini Imerese sits on the Tyrrhenian coast about 35 km east of Palermo. It has a hilltop old town above a harbor. The tree places several families there through the 1700s and 1800s, all of them neighbors and in-laws:

  • the Palmisanos: Fillipo, born 1762, and his son Vincenzo, 1799–1857
  • the Cefalù/Ciofalo family: Gaspare Ciofalo, who died in Termini in 1776
  • the Carusos: Nicolo Caruso and his daughter Rosaria "Rosa", who married Vincenzo Palmisano

Filippo Palmesana was born in January 1846 and emigrated in 1881. His wife Antonia followed in 1885. Their daughter Reosa was born in Kansas City in January 1888. By 1900 the family was in Denver, where Reosa married Joseph Marzyck. She lived in Denver until 1983.

If you are in Sicily: Termini Imerese is the town to visit. Cefalù, one of the island's most visited towns, is 35 km further east along the coast. The tree's Cefalù and Ciofalo ancestors carry its name. The Chiesa Madre (mother church) of Termini Imerese holds the parish registers where these baptisms and marriages would have been recorded.

What's proven: Filippo and Antonia's arrival and Reosa's American life are documented by censuses. The tree links Filippo to the Termini Imerese Palmisanos, but that link needs his Italian birth record; the Antenati portal (antenati.cultura.gov.it) has free scans of Sicilian civil records from 1820 on. A further line from Carini, back to the 1500s, depends on an unproven name match and is marked as such.

stories.title: Two families from Vienna
stories.dek: The Marzycks and the Papesches both came from Vienna, sixty years apart. They met in America.
stories.html:
John Marzyck was born in Vienna about 1810. He went into the "mercantile business" and ended up in Charleston, South Carolina, where he died of consumption (tuberculosis) in November 1868. His son Charles Francis Marzyck was born in Austria in 1851. Charles was naturalized in Colorado and lived in Denver with his Prussian-born wife, Mary Kasner. He died in San Francisco in 1910.

Their son Joseph, born in Colorado in 1887, made the Denver Post on 17 November 1906, at age 19, for losing his money. The clipping is attached to his record on Ancestry. Joseph married Reosa Palmesana, the daughter of Sicilian immigrants, and their daughter Mary Agnes was born in Denver in 1907.

Viktor Papesch was born in Vienna on 26 January 1905. He arrived in New York on 26 July 1930 and became a U.S. citizen in 1936. By 1940 he was living in Chicago with Mary Agnes and their son Roger. In 1955 Viktor made a trip back to Europe through Cherbourg and Le Havre. He lived to 101 and died in Wilmette, Illinois, in 2006. Mary Agnes died there two years later.

What's proven: Censuses, passenger lists, naturalization papers and Social Security records back up this story. Viktor's parents are listed as Ottokar Papesch and a woman whose surname was Hrdlička. Vienna's parish records would tell us more about them.

stories.title: The Polish families of Chicago
stories.dek: Three families sailed to Chicago between 1890 and 1910 and settled within a few miles of each other.
stories.html:
Teofil Pajrowski and his wife Joanna arrived from Poland in 1890 or 1891. Their daughter Sophie was born in Illinois in May 1891, soon after they arrived. They lived in Chicago's 16th Ward, on the Northwest Side.

William Kulik came over as a teenager between 1904 and 1907. His mother Albina arrived in 1904. William married Sophie, and their daughter Ester was born in Chicago in 1916.

Jan (John) Rusin sailed from Antwerp and landed in New York on 14 May 1907, at age 16. Katarzyna "Katie" Rapta made the same crossing in March 1910. Their records list them as Polish but also mention Austria. At the time there was no Polish state, and southern Poland (Galicia) was part of the Austrian Empire. They married in Chicago, and their son Frank was born on Christmas Day 1915.

Frank married Ester Kulik. In 1940 they were living in Leyden Township, west of the city, with their daughter Elaine. Elaine married Roger Papesch in 1960.

What's proven: Censuses, passenger lists, draft cards and naturalization indexes back up this story. The towns the families came from are the next thing to find: "Zlotnov" for Teofil and "Taine" for Albina, as the records spell them. Naturalization papers usually name the hometown.

stories.title: From Dorset to Texas
stories.dek: Martha Bell Palmer was born in a Dorset village where her mother's family had lived for three hundred years. She died in Texas.
stories.html:
The Lodders of Stour Provost, in north Dorset, are the deepest-rooted family in the tree. Three generations in a row named a son Gilbert:

  • Gilbert, born 1629
  • Gilbert, born 1666
  • Gilbert, born 1704

Their descendants George and Thomas Lodder stayed on the same land. Thomas's daughter Elizabeth, born in 1807, married John Palmer of nearby Child Okeford in 1829.

Their daughter Martha Bell Palmer was born at Iwerne Minster in October 1838. At some point after that the family crossed the Atlantic. By 1858 Martha was in Macoupin County, Illinois, where she married Joseph Cullen Drake. Her father died in Macoupin County before 1870. Martha and Joseph eventually moved on to Texas. She died at Goldthwaite, in Mills County, in 1927, aged 88.

Open question: The tree has Martha's mother, Elizabeth, dying in Bath, England, in 1875. Did she go back to England, or is that a different Elizabeth Palmer? A passenger list for the family's crossing would answer it.

What's proven: None of these Dorset records cite a source yet. The Dorset History Centre holds the Stour Provost and Iwerne Minster parish registers. The oldest Lodder generations have a surname mix-up (Lodder and Metyard) that needs sorting out first.
